flashcards.q: What's the difference between the single-skill design question and the corpus-level design question?
flashcards.a: Single-skill: does it fire correctly (trigger accuracy + output quality). Corpus: does it stay ONE coherent system as it grows -- composition, description collisions, and shared invariants across many independently-authored skills.

flashcards.q: What is the reported token-budget payoff of progressive disclosure vs a monolithic system prompt?
flashcards.a: 30-50% reduction in planning errors, 16+ percentage-point improvement in task completion, and 3-8x context-budget efficiency, measured on corpora in the tens-of-skills range.

flashcards.q: Roughly what does listing one skill cost, and what does invoking its body cost?
flashcards.a: ~100 tokens for name+description in the listing, paid every session regardless of use. Up to ~5,000 tokens for the body, paid only when the skill actually matches and loads.

flashcards.q: Name the four composition patterns for a skill corpus.
flashcards.a: Serial (A's output feeds B's input), parallel (independent skills, no ordering constraint), conditional routing (one skill's when_to_use defers to another via negative space), and recursive/nested invocation (a skill forks a subagent that preloads other skills).

flashcards.q: Which composition pattern scales best across a growing skill corpus, and why?
flashcards.a: Serial composition through a shared artifact on disk, not a direct call -- it doesn't require skill A to know skill B exists, only that both agree on the artifact's shape, which is much looser and more durable coupling.

flashcards.q: Name the corpus-scale failure mode distinct from a single skill never firing or firing too eagerly.
flashcards.a: Description collision: two independently-authored skills' descriptions overlap enough that the same or similar request fires a different skill on different sessions, even though each skill individually passes its own trigger-accuracy test.

flashcards.q: How do you detect description collision across a skill corpus?
flashcards.a: Run every skill's should-trigger prompt set against the WHOLE corpus, not just its own skill, and flag any prompt that fires more than one skill. Passing your own trigger test says nothing about colliding with a neighbor.

flashcards.q: How does the value (and risk) of a skill corpus scale with its size?
flashcards.a: Combinatorially, not linearly -- n skills create up to n(n-1)/2 possible two-skill compositions, and the same arithmetic applies to possible pairwise description collisions.

flashcards.q: In this repo's skills/ reference architecture, what does 'repo-as-source-of-truth with an install step' mean concretely?
flashcards.a: SKILL.md files live in the repo, versioned with the content they operate on; install.ps1 does an explicit, one-way, re-runnable copy into ~/.claude/skills/ so they work in any session, with the account copy explicitly documented as NOT tracking the repo (must re-sync after edits).

flashcards.q: What is the 'fragments-not-aggregates' invariant in this repo's skill corpus, and why does it matter architecturally?
flashcards.a: Every content-writing skill writes its own fragment file (app/data/cards/<id>.json, drillsets/<id>.json) -- never hand-edits the generated aggregates. A build step merges by id. This lets 12 independently-invoked skills run in any order with no race on shared output.

flashcards.q: What is the weakest link in this repo's fragments-not-aggregates invariant?
flashcards.a: It's enforced only by documentation (a README rule), not by code -- Level 1 instruction, not Level 3 enforcement. Nothing stops a new skill from hand-editing the aggregate directly except convention.

flashcards.q: Why should each skill in a corpus point at a shared spec rather than restate its format?
flashcards.a: If the format changes, only the spec needs updating; skills describing HOW to use it (not WHAT it currently says) stay correct without modification. Duplicating a fact a dozen skills depend on means an edit can silently desync the rest.

flashcards.q: How does a skill's cost contract change when it's preloaded into a forked subagent vs the regular session?
flashcards.a: A subagent's preloaded skills inject FULL content at startup, unlike the regular session's progressive name+description listing. A skill that's cheap in the main session can be a real cold-start cost once nested.

flashcards.q: Is a marketplace with 800,000+ community-contributed skills evidence of ecosystem quality?
flashcards.a: It's strong evidence the FORMAT achieved cross-tool adoption, not evidence about the quality or safety of any individual skill -- a checked-in skill can still grant itself broad tool access, and marketplace scale has no uniform review bar.

flashcards.q: When is a skill-mediated architecture the wrong system design at the corpus level?
flashcards.a: When most capability is unconditional (belongs in a rules file) or deterministic-and-fragile (belongs in scripts/tools behind a thin judgment layer). A corpus padded with misclassified content dilutes listing budget for the few skills that actually need progressive disclosure.
